# Trees, forests and boosting

::: {.column-margin}
**Margin legend**

**KEY** — a central idea to remember.

**↪** — link to another chapter or lecture.

**⚠** — common pitfall or point of caution.

## Where this chapter fits

Day 7 delivered two tools and left them without an application
that needed them. The bootstrap was demonstrated on a slope for which a formula
already existed; cross-validation was demonstrated on a polynomial whose degree
could almost have been chosen by eye. Both were introduced on models simple
enough to check. This chapter is where they become load-bearing.

A regression tree has no coefficient table, no residual degrees of freedom, and
no parameter count that measures its flexibility. The question of how large to
grow it therefore cannot be answered by an information criterion in the routine
way; it is answered by cross-validation. A single tree is also strikingly
unstable: refit it on a resampled data set and it changes shape. That
instability, which would ordinarily be a fatal defect, turns out to be the raw
material for the most successful family of predictive methods in applied
statistics — because the bootstrap can average it away.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Bagging is the bootstrap applied not to measure variance but to
destroy it. Day 7 built the machine; this chapter puts it to
work.
:::

The arc runs from a single tree, through its weaknesses, to three distinct
repairs. Bagging averages many trees grown on bootstrap resamples. Random
forests improve on bagging by making the trees less alike. Boosting abandons
averaging altogether and grows trees in sequence, each one correcting its
predecessors. The three differ in what part of the error they attack, and that
difference is the organising idea of the second half.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** ISLR Chapter 8 covers the same ground. A reading guide with figure and
page numbers is given at the end of this chapter.
:::

## Explaining variance by splitting

### The idea

Every method in the course so far has explained variation in a response by
writing it as a function of the predictors: a line, a curve, a link function
applied to a linear predictor. A tree does something different and cruder. It
partitions the predictor space into rectangular regions and predicts a single
constant within each one.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — A **regression tree** partitions the predictor space into
non-overlapping regions $R_1, \dots, R_J$ and predicts, for any observation
falling in $R_j$, the mean of the training responses in that region.
:::

The connection to the rest of the course is the variance partition of Day 1.
A split is accepted when the combined within-group sum of squares of the two
resulting subsets is smaller than that of the parent. This is the quantity that
one-way ANOVA minimises when it assigns observations to known groups; the tree
differs only in that it also chooses the groups.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** Day 1 partitioned total variance into a part explained by the model
and a residual. A tree does the same, but searches for the partition rather than
being handed it by the design.
:::

### A simulated forest-floor survey

We simulate a survey of understorey vegetation in 400 forest plots. The
predictors are canopy openness, soil moisture, soil pH and litter depth, plus
two variables that carry no signal at all and are included so that we can see
what each method does with them.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(8)

n <- 400
plots <- data.frame(
  light    = runif(n, 0.02, 0.80),   # canopy openness (proportion)
  moisture = runif(n, 10, 45),       # soil moisture (%)
  pH       = runif(n, 3.8, 7.2),
  litter   = runif(n, 0, 8),         # litter depth (cm)
  noise1   = runif(n, 0, 1),         # no effect
  noise2   = rnorm(n)                # no effect
)

wet <- plots$moisture >= 25

mu <- 18 +
      35 * plots$light * wet +       # light helps only where moisture allows
      12 * (plots$pH > 5.5) +        # a step, not a gradient
      -1.5 * plots$litter            # a genuine linear effect

plots$cover <- mu + rnorm(n, 0, 6)   # herb cover (%)

summary(plots$cover)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.3449 16.2407 24.4531 25.6474 34.5900 64.0183
```


:::
:::




The generating process is deliberately awkward for a linear model and
comfortable for a tree. Canopy openness raises herb cover, but only in plots
with at least 25% soil moisture: in dry plots extra light does nothing. Soil pH
acts as a step at 5.5 rather than as a gradient. Litter depth alone enters
linearly. The residual distribution has mean 0 and variance $6^2 = 36$, which is
the irreducible error that no method can beat.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Two of the three structures — an interaction and a threshold — are
exactly what a rectangular partition represents naturally and an additive linear
model represents badly.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
eta <- -1.8 +
       4.0 * plots$light * wet +
       1.2 * (plots$pH > 5.5) +
       -0.15 * plots$litter

plots$p_true <- plogis(eta)
plots$moss   <- factor(rbinom(n, 1, plots$p_true), labels = c("absent", "present"))

table(plots$moss)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#>  absent present 
#>     270     130
```


:::
:::




The same plots also carry a binary response: presence of an indicator moss,
generated from a logistic model driven by the same threshold structure. Because
the true probability of presence is stored in `p_true`, we will later be able to
compute the best performance any classifier could possibly achieve.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** `p_true` is in the data frame, so a formula written as `moss ~ .` would
include the true probability as a predictor and produce a flawless classifier
that has learned nothing. Every model below uses an explicit formula. Leakage of
this kind is rarely so obvious in real data — an identifier correlated with
treatment, or a variable measured after the outcome, does the same damage
quietly.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f_reg <- cover ~ light + moisture + pH + litter + noise1 + noise2
f_cls <- moss  ~ light + moisture + pH + litter + noise1 + noise2
```
:::

The additive linear model recovers a positive light effect, a positive moisture
effect and a negative litter effect. None of these is wrong, and none of them is
the structure that generated the data. An additive model has no way to represent
"light matters only when moisture exceeds 25%"; it can only report an average
light effect taken across wet and dry plots, which is too small in the wet plots
and too large in the dry ones. Nor can it represent a step: a linear pH term
spreads a discontinuity at 5.5 across the whole pH range.

The remedy within the linear framework is to specify the interaction and the
threshold explicitly. That requires knowing they are there. A tree searches for
them.

### Recursive binary splitting

The algorithm is a greedy search. At each node, every predictor and every
candidate split point is considered; the split chosen is the one that most
reduces the residual sum of squares,

$$
\sum_{i \in R_{\text{left}}} (y_i - \bar y_{\text{left}})^2 +
\sum_{i \in R_{\text{right}}} (y_i - \bar y_{\text{right}})^2 ,
$$

and the procedure then repeats within each of the two children until a stopping
rule intervenes.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — The search is **greedy** because it takes the best split available
now, without considering whether a worse split now would permit a better pair of
splits later. The globally optimal tree is not found, and is not sought.
:::

Two properties follow immediately from the algorithm and are worth stating
before any code is run. Predictors are never transformed and never scaled,
because only the *order* of a numeric predictor matters to a split point: any
monotone transformation of a predictor leaves the tree unchanged. And
interactions are represented without being specified, because a split made below
another split applies only within that branch.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** The converse of scale invariance is that a tree cannot extrapolate. Every
prediction is an average of training observations, so predicted values are
bounded by the range of the observed response. A tree fitted to plots with up to
60% cover will never predict 80%, whatever the predictors say.
:::




::: {.cell}

### The split search, from scratch

The search for the best split looks expensive: for every candidate cut-point, two means and two sums of squares. It is cheap, because of an identity. Splitting a node of $n$ observations into a left part of $n_L$ and a right part of $n_R$ reduces the residual sum of squares by

$$
\text{RSS}_{\text{parent}} - \big(\text{RSS}_L + \text{RSS}_R\big) = \frac{n_L\,n_R}{n}\,\big(\bar y_L - \bar y_R\big)^2 .
$$

This is the between-group sum of squares of Day 1 for two groups. The gain is large when the two means differ strongly *and* both parts are reasonably large; the factor $n_Ln_R/n$ is what discourages splitting off a single extreme point. Only the two means are needed, and after sorting the predictor once they are available for every cut-point from a running sum.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
best_split <- function(x, y) {
  o <- order(x); x <- x[o]; y <- y[o]
  n  <- length(y)
  nL <- 1:(n - 1); nR <- n - nL                  # sizes for every possible cut
  sL <- cumsum(y)[nL]; sR <- sum(y) - sL         # running sums give the two means
  gain <- nL * nR / n * (sL / nL - sR / nR)^2    # reduction in RSS
  gain[x[nL] == x[nL + 1]] <- -Inf               # cannot cut between equal values
  i <- which.max(gain)
  c(cut = (x[i] + x[i + 1]) / 2, gain = gain[i])
}

vars <- all.vars(f_reg)[-1]
round(t(sapply(plots[vars], best_split, y = plots$cover)), 2)
```

## Growing and pruning

### Why the unpruned tree is a saturated model

Left alone, recursive splitting continues until every leaf holds a single
observation. At that point the training residual sum of squares is zero and the
tree reproduces the data exactly. Day 1 named this situation: a model with
as many parameters as observations has no residual degrees of freedom, fits
perfectly, and reveals nothing about the population.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — A fully grown tree is the saturated model of Day 1 arrived at by a
different route. The problem is the same and so is the diagnosis; only the
remedy is new, because the flexibility of a tree cannot be counted in
parameters.
:::

The difficulty is that the number of leaves is not a usable parameter count. A
tree with eight leaves has consumed far more than eight degrees of freedom,
because the split points and split variables were themselves chosen by searching
the data. There is no simple correction, which is why AIC is not the tool here.

### Cost-complexity pruning

The standard approach grows a large tree deliberately and then removes branches,
trading fit against size. For a tree $T$ with $|T|$ terminal nodes, define

$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha \, |T|,
$$

where $R(T)$ is the training error — the residual sum of squares for a
regression tree — and $\alpha \ge 0$ is the complexity parameter. For each value
of $\alpha$ there is a unique smallest subtree minimising $R_\alpha$, and as
$\alpha$ increases the sequence of these subtrees is nested: branches are pruned
away in a fixed order, never rearranged.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — `rpart` reports a scaled version of $\alpha$ called **`cp`**, expressed
relative to the error of the root-only tree. A split is attempted only if it
improves the relative error by at least `cp`.
:::

Pruning backwards rather than stopping early matters. A split that appears weak can enable a highly informative split beneath it. In our simulation the split on moisture is useful in itself, but much of its value lies in the light split it makes possible in the wet branch. A rule that judged every split only by its immediate gain would undervalue that structure.

## Classification trees

### The same algorithm, a different criterion

For a categorical response the partition is built in exactly the same way, and
only the quantity minimised changes. A leaf predicts the majority class among
its training observations, and reports the class proportions alongside it.

Three measures of node impurity are in use. For a node $m$ with class
proportions $\hat p_{mk}$:

$$
\text{misclassification error} \quad E = 1 - \max_k \hat p_{mk},
$$
$$
\text{Gini index} \quad G = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk} (1 - \hat p_{mk}),
$$
$$
\text{cross-entropy} \quad D = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} \hat p_{mk} \log \hat p_{mk}.
$$

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** Cross-entropy is the Shannon entropy of the class distribution within the
node. Day 5 introduced it and
connected it to deviance and AIC.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
p <- seq(0.0005, 0.9995, length.out = 600)

gini <- 2 * p * (1 - p)
ent  <- -(p * log2(p) + (1 - p) * log2(1 - p)) / 2
err  <- pmin(p, 1 - p)

plot(p, ent, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick", ylim = c(0, 0.55),
     xlab = expression(hat(p)), ylab = "impurity")
lines(p, gini, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
lines(p, err,  lwd = 2, col = "grey35", lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 1, 1),
       col = c("grey35", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("misclassification error", "Gini index",
                  "cross-entropy (halved)"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three node-impurity measures for a two-class node, as a function of the proportion of the first class. Cross-entropy is halved so that all three share the same maximum. The misclassification rate is piecewise linear and has zero gradient nowhere except at its peak.](10-trees-forests_files/figure-html/fig-impurity-1.png){#fig-impurity width=624}
:::
:::




The figure explains why trees are grown with Gini or entropy rather than with
the error rate. All three are zero at a pure node and maximal at an even split,
but the error rate is piecewise linear: splitting a node with proportions
$(0.8, 0.2)$ into two children with proportions $(0.9, 0.1)$ and $(0.7, 0.3)$
leaves the total error rate unchanged, so the split appears worthless. Gini and
entropy are strictly concave and reward the increase in purity. The error rate
is nevertheless the right criterion for *pruning*, where predictive accuracy is
the target.

The claim about the $(0.8, 0.2)$ node is easily checked. The split produces two children of equal size.

## A single tree is a weak learner

### Instability

The defect that motivates everything in the rest of the chapter is easiest to
see than to describe. We refit the tree on four bootstrap resamples of the same
data.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — A **weak learner** performs only slightly better than a trivial
baseline: better than chance for classification, better than the intercept-only
model for regression. Weakness is not a disqualification; it is the input to an
ensemble.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(562)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

for (b in 1:4) {
  boot_rows <- sample(nrow(plots), replace = TRUE)
  tree_b <- rpart(f_reg, data = plots[boot_rows, ], method = "anova",
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.03))
  draw_tree(tree_b, type = 2, extra = 0, tweak = 1.1,
             box.palette = "Blues", main = paste("resample", b))
}
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](10-trees-forests_files/figure-html/instability-1.png){width=864}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(op)
```
:::




The four trees are fitted to data sets that differ only through resampling, and
yet they differ in which variable is split first, where the split points fall,
and sometimes in which variables appear at all. The greedy search is the cause:
once the root split changes, everything beneath it is fitted to different
subsets, so a small perturbation near the top propagates into a completely
different structure.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** The instability is a property of the fitted structure, not necessarily of
the predictions. Two visibly different trees may predict similarly. The
consequence is that the *interpretation* of a single tree — "pH is the most
important variable, and the cutoff is 5.5" — is far less reliable than it looks.
:::

### The variance problem, stated

In the language of the bias–variance decomposition, a deep tree has low bias and
high variance. It can approximate almost any structure given enough splits, so
it is not systematically wrong; but the particular structure it produces depends
heavily on the particular sample, so it is unreliable.

High variance is the easier of the two problems to attack, because variance is
reduced by averaging. If $B$ independent estimates each have variance
$\sigma^2$, their mean has variance $\sigma^2 / B$. The obstacle is that we have
only one data set and therefore only one tree. That obstacle was removed on
Day 7.

## Bagging

### Bootstrap aggregating

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Bagging** draws $B$ bootstrap resamples of the training data, fits a
deep unpruned tree to each, and averages their predictions (for regression) or
takes a majority vote (for classification).
:::

$$
\hat f_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} \hat f^{\,b}(x)
$$

Two details of the recipe deserve attention. The individual trees are grown
*deep and unpruned*: pruning would reduce their variance, but variance is what
the averaging is for, and pruning would raise their bias, which averaging cannot
repair. And $B$ is not a tuning parameter. Increasing it can only reduce the
variance of the ensemble, so it is set as large as the computing budget allows
and never chosen by cross-validation.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** Day 7 established that a bootstrap resample
omits about 37% of the rows. Those omitted rows are about to become useful.
:::

### Why the trees must differ

The averaging argument above assumed independence, which bootstrap resamples of
one data set certainly are not: they share most of their rows. If the individual
predictions have variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$, the
variance of their average is

$$
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat f_{\text{bag}}\right)
  = \sigma^2 \left( \rho + \frac{1 - \rho}{B} \right).
$$

The formula follows from the three lines that gave the design effect on Day 7. The variance of a sum is the sum of all variances and covariances. There are $B$ variances $\sigma^2$ and $B(B-1)$ covariances $\rho\sigma^2$, so

$$
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B \hat f^{\,b}\right)
= \frac{1}{B^2}\Big[B\,\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\,\rho\,\sigma^2\Big]
= \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{(1-\rho)\,\sigma^2}{B} .
$$

Correlated trees are the clustered observations of Day 7 in a new guise: a hundred trees that all make the same mistake carry the information of one.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
B_seq <- 1:200
rhos  <- c(0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
cols  <- c("grey25", "steelblue", "darkorange3", "firebrick")

plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 200), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "number of trees, B",
     ylab = expression(Var(bar(f)) / sigma^2))
for (i in seq_along(rhos)) {
  lines(B_seq, rhos[i] + (1 - rhos[i]) / B_seq, lwd = 2, col = cols[i])
  abline(h = rhos[i], lty = 3, col = cols[i])
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = cols,
       legend = paste("rho =", rhos))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Variance of an ensemble average, relative to the variance of a single member, as the number of members grows. Each curve is a different pairwise correlation between members. The second term vanishes with B; the first does not.](10-trees-forests_files/figure-html/fig-bagvar-1.png){#fig-bagvar width=624}
:::
:::




The figure contains the entire argument for random forests. The second term
falls away as $B$ grows, but the first does not: the ensemble variance has a
floor at $\rho \sigma^2$, however many trees are grown. Adding trees beyond a
few hundred is therefore pointless, and the only remaining way to improve the
ensemble is to reduce the correlation between its members.

Correlation between bagged trees is high whenever one predictor dominates,
because every resample will choose it for the root split and the trees will all
share their most consequential decision.

### Out-of-bag error

Setting `mtry` equal to the number of predictors — all six here — means every

The printed "Mean of squared residuals" is not a training error. It is the
**out-of-bag** error: for each observation, the prediction is averaged over only
those trees whose bootstrap sample excluded it, so every prediction is made by
trees that never saw that observation. About a third of the ensemble contributes
to each OOB prediction.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Out-of-bag error is cross-validation that costs nothing. It comes free
with the resampling that bagging performs anyway, and for large $B$ it is close
to the leave-one-out cross-validated error.

### What bagging costs

The ensemble no longer has a picture. There is no single tree to plot, no set of
decision rules to quote, and no cutoff to report. Bagging buys accuracy with
interpretability, and this is the point at which tree-based methods stop being
an exploratory tool and become a predictive one.

Something interpretable can still be recovered, in the form of variable
importance, which is developed in the next section because it matters equally
for random forests.

## Random forests

### Decorrelating the trees

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — A **random forest** is bagging with one modification: at each split,
only a random subset of $m$ of the $p$ predictors is considered as a candidate.
A fresh subset is drawn at every split of every tree.
:::

The modification looks perverse — the algorithm is forbidden from using the best
variable at most splits — and it works for the reason @fig-bagvar makes visible.
If a dominant predictor is unavailable at a given split, the tree is forced to
use something else, so trees stop making the same decisions. The correlation
$\rho$ falls, the floor of the variance curve drops, and the ensemble improves
even though every individual member has become slightly worse.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Random forests trade a small increase in the bias of each tree for a
large reduction in the correlation between them. This is the only place in the
course where deliberately weakening the components improves the whole.
:::

Conventional defaults are $m \approx \sqrt{p}$ for classification and
$m \approx p/3$ for regression. Unlike $B$, $m$ is a genuine tuning parameter
and is worth cross-validating: small $m$ gives maximal decorrelation and maximal
individual bias, large $m$ returns to bagging.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

                       importance = TRUE)

c(bagging_oob_mse = tail(bag_fit$mse, 1),
  forest_oob_mse  = tail(rf_fit$mse, 1),
  irreducible     = 36)
```

## Boosting

Bagging and random forests start from deep trees and remove their variance by averaging. Boosting does the opposite: it starts from very small trees and removes their bias by accumulation. It uses the same simulated survey of understorey vegetation.

### Sequential correction

Bagging and random forests fit their trees independently and in parallel; each
one sees the data afresh. Boosting does the opposite. Trees are fitted in
sequence, and each one is fitted to what the current ensemble is still getting
wrong.

::: {.column-margin}
**DEF** — **Boosting** builds an additive model by repeatedly fitting a small
tree to the current residuals and adding a shrunken version of it to the running
prediction.
:::

For regression with squared-error loss the algorithm is short enough to state in
full. Set $\hat f(x) = 0$ and $r_i = y_i$. Then for $b = 1, \dots, B$:

1. fit a tree $\hat f^{\,b}$ with $d$ splits to the current residuals $r$;
2. update the prediction, $\hat f(x) \leftarrow \hat f(x) + \lambda \hat f^{\,b}(x)$;
3. update the residuals, $r_i \leftarrow r_i - \lambda \hat f^{\,b}(x_i)$.

The output is $\hat f(x) = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \lambda \hat f^{\,b}(x)$.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** This is ISLR Algorithm 8.2, page 347. For other loss functions the
residual is replaced by the negative gradient of the loss, which is where the
name *gradient boosting* comes from.
:::

The learning is deliberately slow. Each tree is small, and only a fraction
$\lambda$ of it is added, so no single step commits the model to much. Fitting
the residuals means that regions already predicted well contribute nothing
further, and attention concentrates automatically where the ensemble is still
failing.

### Boosting is gradient descent in function space

Why fit the *residuals*? The answer connects boosting to the gradient descent of Appendix C. Suppose the aim is to minimise a loss summed over the training data,

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n L\big(y_i,\ f(x_i)\big),
$$

and regard the fitted values $f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)$ as the quantities to be adjusted. Gradient descent would move each of them a small step against its derivative:

$$
f(x_i) \leftarrow f(x_i) - \lambda\,g_i,
\qquad
g_i = \frac{\partial L\big(y_i, f(x_i)\big)}{\partial f(x_i)} .
$$

For squared-error loss $L = \tfrac12(y - f)^2$ the negative gradient is

$$
-g_i = y_i - f(x_i),
$$

the residual. The catch is that such a step is defined only at the training points and says nothing about a new $x$. Boosting therefore fits a small tree *to the negative gradients* and steps along that tree instead. The tree generalises the step to the whole predictor space.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Each boosting round is one step of gradient descent, with a tree standing in for the gradient. The shrinkage $\lambda$ is the step size.
:::

The same recipe works for any differentiable loss, and only the "pseudo-residuals" change.

| Loss | $L(y, f)$ | Negative gradient $-g_i$ |
|:--|:--|:--|
| squared error | $\tfrac12(y - f)^2$ | $y_i - f(x_i)$ |
| absolute error | $\lvert y - f\rvert$ | $\operatorname{sign}\big(y_i - f(x_i)\big)$ |
| logistic (0/1 labels, $f$ = log-odds) | $-yf + \ln(1 + e^{f})$ | $y_i - p_i$ |

The last row is the gradient of the logistic log-likelihood of Day 6: a boosted classifier fits trees to $y_i - p_i$.

### Boosting from scratch

With `rpart` supplying the small trees, the algorithm is a loop of a few lines. One hundred plots are set aside to watch the error on data the model has not seen.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(104)
test_id <- sample(nrow(plots), 100)
b_train <- plots[-test_id, ]
b_test  <- plots[test_id, ]

boost_scratch <- function(train, test, B = 600, shrink = 0.05, depth = 2) {
  f_train <- rep(mean(train$cover), nrow(train))        # start from the mean
  f_test  <- rep(mean(train$cover), nrow(test))
  err <- matrix(NA, B, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("train", "test")))
  work <- train
  for (b in seq_len(B)) {
    work$r <- train$cover - f_train                     # 1. residuals = negative gradient
    tree <- rpart(r ~ light + moisture + pH + litter + noise1 + noise2, data = work,
                  control = rpart.control(maxdepth = depth, cp = 0, minbucket = 10, xval = 0))
    f_train <- f_train + shrink * predict(tree, train)  # 2. take a small step
    f_test  <- f_test  + shrink * predict(tree, test)
    err[b, ] <- c(mean((train$cover - f_train)^2), mean((test$cover - f_test)^2))
  }
  err
}

err <- boost_scratch(b_train, b_test)

plot(err[, "train"], type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue", ylim = c(0, 160),
     xlab = "Boosting round", ylab = "Mean squared error")
lines(err[, "test"], lwd = 2)
abline(h = 36, lty = 3, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = which.min(err[, "test"]), lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topright", c("held-out plots", "training plots", "irreducible error"), bty = "n",
       lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 1, 3), col = c("black", "steelblue", "firebrick"))
```

### Three tuning parameters

Boosting has three parameters, and in contrast to bagging all three matter.

The **number of trees** $B$ must be chosen, because boosting *can* overfit if it
is too large. This is the sharpest contrast with random forests, where more
trees are never harmful. Each additional boosting round makes the model more
flexible; each additional forest member only averages away more variance.

The **shrinkage** $\lambda$, typically 0.01 or 0.001, controls how much of each
tree is taken. Smaller $\lambda$ requires larger $B$; the two trade off against
each other and are usually chosen together.

The **interaction depth** $d$ is the number of splits per tree. With $d = 1$
each tree is a stump involving a single variable, and the boosted ensemble is
then an additive model with no interactions at all. With $d = 2$ pairwise
interactions become representable, and so on: $d$ is the interaction order of
the fitted model, chosen rather than specified term by term.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — In our simulation the generating process contains one two-way
interaction, so $d = 2$ is sufficient in principle and $d = 1$ is not. Boosting
makes the interaction order an explicit, tunable quantity.
:::




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gbm)

set.seed(104)
boost_fit <- gbm(f_reg, data = plots, distribution = "gaussian",
                 n.trees = 3000, interaction.depth = 2,
                 shrinkage = 0.01, n.minobsinnode = 10,
                 cv.folds = 5)

best_iter <- gbm.perf(boost_fit, method = "cv")
```

## Bias, variance, and which method attacks which

The three ensembles are often presented as interchangeable alternatives. They
are not, and the distinction is the single most useful thing to remember from
this chapter.

| | Bagging | Random forest | Boosting |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Attacks | variance | variance | bias |
| Base learners | deep, unpruned | deep, unpruned | shallow, often stumps |
| Fitted | in parallel, independently | in parallel, decorrelated | sequentially, dependently |
| Effect of large $B$ | never harmful | never harmful | can overfit |
| Tuning needed | little | `mtry` | $B$, $\lambda$, $d$ — all three |
| Built-in validation | out-of-bag | out-of-bag | none; use CV |
| Interpretability | low | low, plus importance | low, plus relative influence |

Bagging and random forests start from a low-bias, high-variance learner and
remove the variance by averaging. Boosting starts from a high-bias,
low-variance learner — a stump is about as biased as a model can be — and
removes the bias by accumulation. Reading the table row by row, almost every
difference between the columns follows from that one difference in the first
row.

## An honest comparison

Everything so far has been demonstrated on in-sample output or on out-of-bag
error. The methods are now compared on equal terms, under one set of
cross-validation folds, with all tuning performed inside the training data.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
k <- 5
set.seed(77)
fold <- cut(sample(seq_len(nrow(plots))), breaks = k, labels = FALSE)

methods <- c("linear model", "pruned tree", "bagging",
             "random forest", "boosting")
mse <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = k, ncol = length(methods),
              dimnames = list(NULL, methods))

for (j in seq_len(k)) {
  train <- plots[fold != j, ]
  test  <- plots[fold == j, ]

  m_lm <- lm(f_reg, data = train)
  mse[j, "linear model"] <- mean((predict(m_lm, test) - test$cover)^2)

  m_tr <- rpart(f_reg, data = train, method = "anova",
                control = rpart.control(cp = 0.002, minsplit = 10, xval = 10))
  cp_j <- m_tr$cptable[which.min(m_tr$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
  m_tr <- prune(m_tr, cp = cp_j)
  mse[j, "pruned tree"] <- mean((predict(m_tr, test) - test$cover)^2)

  m_bag <- randomForest(f_reg, data = train, mtry = 6, ntree = 300)
  mse[j, "bagging"] <- mean((predict(m_bag, test) - test$cover)^2)

  m_rf <- randomForest(f_reg, data = train, mtry = 2, ntree = 300)
  mse[j, "random forest"] <- mean((predict(m_rf, test) - test$cover)^2)

  m_gb <- gbm(f_reg, data = train, distribution = "gaussian",
              n.trees = 1500, interaction.depth = 2, shrinkage = 0.02,
              n.minobsinnode = 10, cv.folds = 5)
  it_j <- gbm.perf(m_gb, method = "cv", plot.it = FALSE)
  mse[j, "boosting"] <- mean((predict(m_gb, test, n.trees = it_j) -
                                test$cover)^2)
}

round(rbind(CV_MSE = colMeans(mse),
            SE     = apply(mse, 2, sd) / sqrt(k)), 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        linear model pruned tree bagging random forest boosting
#> CV_MSE        79.01       58.18   52.13         51.69    45.72
#> SE             5.07        5.06    3.14          3.88     2.96
```


:::
:::




Three points about the design of this comparison matter more than the numbers it
produces.

First, it is a **nested** cross-validation. The `cp` for the tree and the
iteration count for the boosted model are selected by cross-validation *within*
each training fold — `rpart` does this internally through `xval`, and `gbm`
through `cv.folds`. The outer folds never participate in any choice, so the
reported errors are honest estimates of the whole procedure.

::: {.column-margin}
**↪** Day 7 argued for exactly this structure. The
inner loops here are supplied by the fitting functions rather than written out,
but they are the same construction.
:::

Second, the standard errors across folds are reported alongside the means. With
five folds these are crude, and differences smaller than a couple of standard
errors should not be read as a ranking. The one-standard-error rule applies to
method comparison just as it applied to tree size.

Third, every error should be read against the irreducible error of 36. A method
achieving 45 has captured most of the available structure; the remaining gap to
another method achieving 42 is a small fraction of what either has already
explained. Improvements look larger than they are when the floor is forgotten.

::: {.column-margin}
**⚠** If the plots had been nested within forest stands, every fold above would
have to be grouped by stand. Ensembles are especially vulnerable to this leak: a
deep tree can effectively memorise a stand, so random folds would report an
error close to the within-stand residual variance and a forest would appear to
outperform everything else for entirely spurious reasons.
:::

essentially a Bayesian treatment of the same additive-tree idea.

## Where this leads

The methods of this chapter produce models that predict well and explain little. That is a genuine change in what a statistical model is for, and it is worth stating plainly. A fitted random forest supports the claim that herb cover can be predicted from these four variables to within a certain error. It does not support a claim about the effect of raising soil pH by one unit, and no amount of variable-importance plotting converts it into one.

::: {.column-margin}
**KEY** — Prediction and explanation are different goals served by different models.
:::

The course began with one proposition: statistics arises the moment a complicated process is described with a simple model. Every method since has been a version of it. Each approximates a process, explains part of the variation, leaves a residual, spends some measure of flexibility, and must be judged on data it has not seen.
